Question: If the universe is expanding faster than light, then can a device that duplicates the effect at least in principle be designed?
Answer: No - to get that effect you need a whole lot of space in between the two points you’re considering the separation of. There’s no way to get it to happen over a smaller distance. Also, please understand that the expansion of space does not involve any objects moving from one place to another. Consider partially inflating a balloon and drawing a pair of dots on it. You can blow the balloon up further and get those dots to move further apart, or let some air out and get them to move closer together. But you can’t cause something sitting on one of the dots to move to the other dot - that’s just not how it works. It’s just not applicable to transportation or communication. Stay safe and well! Question: How do you intuitively explain the twins paradox?
Answer: By noting that it’s not a paradox. People just think it is because they start to tell themselves that you ought to be able to regard either twin as the one stationary and either as the one moving. So how can they be different ages at the end? Well, this is an incorrect way of looking at it. You can draw a single spacetime diagram for the entire experiment that shows the Earth twin as stationary, but you can’t do that for the other twin, because there in the middle of the experiment he or she changes directions. It’s that “bend” in the traveling twin’s spacetime diagram that causes the specific outcome. Because of the way the spacetime interval is calculated, the way to experience the largest amount of proper time when moving between two events A and B is to move between them in a straight line on the Minkowski diagram. If you follow a bent path, you will wind up with less proper time being experienced. The best way to understand this, of course, is to just get familiar with the math. It’s not hard - this is special relativity we’re talking about - not general relativity. Special relativity really can be completely handled with nothing more than high school algebra. Question: Can quantum entanglement be explained using a 4th dimension of space?
Answer: No, I think the better way to explain it is laid out here in this paper: What you have here is a demonstration that spatial dimensions are “not fundamental.” You don’t need them in order to describe the world. The author begins with a model of reality that consists of only an arbitrary number of real-valued functions of time only. No space presumed to exist a priori. This model can basically describe any universe you can imagine. Then he makes a single assumption: that there exist at least one conserved quantity. Then he proceeds to work out the mathematical consequences of that assumption. What you basically get as consequences is… all of physics. You get relativity, electromagnetism, etc. And, most germane to this discussion, you get space. Behaviors emerge in the math that “look like” things moving around in spatial dimensions. The number of spatial dimensions cannot be entirely arbitrary - some dimension counts just “don’t work.” The smallest number that does work is… three. So, what this means is that you do not have to presume space to be a “pre-existing container” that holds everything that happens. It is an emergent container that is a suitable way to “view” some of the relationships that unfold in the model’s dynamics. Some - but not all. There are relationships among those time-variable state items that have nothing to do with space at all. And that is where we can get entanglement. Entanglement doesn’t need any spatial dimensions to operate - it’s a direct connection between time-dependent state variables. Other relationships can exist alongside it that do involve the spatial dimensions, and those relationships are subject to a speed limit we can call c - this is demonstrated clearly and naturally in the paper. This does not mean that space isn’t real. There it is right in front of us - we clearly perceive it, and we all agree that we perceive it, so it’s real all right. It’s just not fundamental - it doesn’t exist as a predecessor of the “stuff” that we see fill space. Question: Could the concept of a corporeal being such as ourselves be based entirely on a quantum phenomenon?
Answer: All of the “corporeal” aspects of us - the matter, basically, is of course well-explained by our best modern physical theories. On the other hand, our thoughts and minds aren’t really explained at all. People want to say “Oh, well, that just happens in some physical way we don’t understand yet,” and I suppose that’s always possible. The problem, though, is that no one can give even the beginnings of the first idea as to how. It’s something people just take as a given - an act of faith no less profound than acts of faith by those who devoutly hold religious belifs. I’m not so sure - I think there may still be things going on we have altogether no clue about. The idea that mind emerges from physics, is of course a completely valid theory, and people should be pursuing that idea and trying to nail down the particulars. But until they have something a little more promising than just an “Oh, we’re sure of it - trust us” faith-based claim, I prefer to keep an open mind. Stay safe and well!
